I've been farming these 12 mu for 30 years now. Wheat in winter, maize in summer — that's what everyone does in Quzhou, and it works. Last year my wheat did about 500 jin per mu, and the maize did a bit better, around 600 jin. This year I'll do about the same, maybe push a little harder on fertilizer because prices for grain haven't been bad, and my son sends some money back from his factory job.

For the winter wheat, I always rotary till after the maize comes off. I put down one full bag of compound fertilizer per mu — that's 50 jin — and I use improved seed, about 25 jin per mu. At green-up time I top-dress with half a bag of urea per mu, that's about 25 jin. If the wheat looks hungry at jointing, I throw another 10 jin of urea on. That means I'm putting roughly 26 jin of nitrogen, 10 jin of phosphorus, and 8 jin of potassium on each mu over the season. I irrigate three times: once before winter to help it survive, once at jointing, and once when the grain is filling. I spray twice — herbicide early, then a fungicide when I see rust starting on the leaves down by the road. I expect 550 kg per mu if the spring rain cooperates.

For summer maize, I don't till after wheat harvest — there's no time, and the straw is good for the soil. I plant hybrid seed right into the stubble, put down compound fertilizer at planting, then side-dress with urea when the plants are at big trumpet stage. That's about 24 jin nitrogen, 6 jin phosphorus, 6 jin potassium per mu total. I irrigate twice if it's dry — once at the V6 stage and once at tasseling. Two pesticide sprays: one for weeds right after planting, one for borers around tasseling. If things go right, 650 kg per mu is what I hope for.

I spend money carefully because fertilizer isn't cheap, but losing yield is worse than wasting a little urea. I watch what my neighbors do. If Old Wang puts more on, I think about adding a bit too. We all talk at the well.
